subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Regulation of the Skies
description: A fast breakdown of Regulation of the Skies for builders.

hook.text: Today's airspace rules were written for commercial jets and helicopters—not thousands of electric air taxis.

buildup.text: Regulators like the FAA must certify each eVTOL design for safety, a process that takes years.

discovery.text: Low-altitude corridors will need to be carved out over cities, separating air taxis from other aircraft.

twist.text: Automated air traffic management using AI may be the only way to handle thousands of simultaneous flights.

climax.text: Getting the rules right is slower than building the aircraft—regulation, not technology, sets the timeline.

punchline.text: Flying cars are ready before the rules that would let them fly.

quiz.question: What is the biggest bottleneck for eVTOL deployment?

details.summary: As flying cars and air taxis approach reality, aviation regulators must create new rules for low-altitude urban airspace, covering pilot certification, noise limits, and traffic management.
details.whyItMatters: Without clear regulations, eVTOL companies cannot operate commercially. The pace of rule-making will determine when and where urban air mobility becomes a reality.
takeaways: FAA and EASA are developing new aircraft certification rules
Urban airspace management systems are being designed from scratch
Noise limits may restrict where eVTOLs can land and take off

faq.question: Will eVTOL pilots need a standard pilot license?
faq.answer: Regulators are developing a new type of license tailored to eVTOL operations. Requirements will likely be less demanding than a full private pilot license but more rigorous than a drone operator permit.

faq.question: How will air taxis avoid colliding with each other?
faq.answer: Automated traffic management systems will assign corridors and altitudes. Onboard detect-and-avoid sensors provide a safety layer, similar to how ground-based air traffic control works for conventional aircraft.
